register.level: aristocratic but coarse-grained: blunt dismissals and folk proverbs in a titled lady's mouth
register.summary: In her own kitchen she is rough, violent in word and short-tempered ('Pig!', 'chop off her head!'). At the croquet-ground she turns cloyingly affectionate and attaches a 'moral' to everything, delivered with total confidence and no logic. Either way she talks at people, not with them.

examples.text: You don't know much, and that's a fact.
Tut, tut, child! Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it.
Very true, flamingoes and mustard both bite. And the moral of that is—'Birds of a feather flock together.'

catchphrases.text: and the moral of that is—'…'
my dear / you dear old thing

sentence_style.length: the longest average line of the cast (mean 17.8 words): statement plus proverb, statement plus 'and that's a fact'

patterns.rule: Moral-tagging: a remark followed by 'and the moral of that is—' and a proverb that does not fit, sometimes an absurd self-generated one.

examples.text: Ah, well! It means much the same thing, and the moral of that is—'Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves.'
Of course it is, there's a large mustard-mine near here. And the moral of that is—'The more there is of mine, the less there is of yours.'
Just about as much right, as pigs have to fly; and the m—

patterns.rule: Blunt, dismissive clinchers ('and that's why', 'and that's a fact', 'don't bother me') that shut the other person down.

examples.text: It's a Cheshire cat, and that's why. Pig!
Oh, don't bother me, I never could abide figures!
Oh, don't talk about trouble! I make you a present of everything I've said as yet.
If everybody minded their own business, the world would go round a deal faster than it does.
They all can, and most of 'em do.

patterns.rule: Gushing, patronising agreement in the croquet scene ('Very true', 'Right, as usual', 'I quite agree with you'), with endearments.

examples.text: Right, as usual, what a clear way you have of putting things!
You can't think how glad I am to see you again, you dear old thing!

patterns.rule: Violent words used carelessly as household speech (chop off her head, beat him, Pig!); never meant literally (SUP-014 tone).

examples.text: Talking of axes, chop off her head!
Here! you may nurse it a bit, if you like! I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen,
'Tis so, and the moral of that is—'Oh, 'tis love, 'tis love, that makes the world go round!'

address.to_alice: my dear / child / you dear old thing

examples.text: You're thinking about something, my dear, and that makes you forget to talk.

forbidden_words.regex: \b(please|sorry|beg (your )?pardon|I'm afraid|I wonder|I don't know|I'm not sure|excuse me)\b
forbidden_words.reason: she is never unsure and never apologises: no softener in her 22 spoken lines; even a missing moral is deferred ('I shall remember it in a bit')
figures are what she 'never could abide'; exact knowledge is Alice's register

drift.change: Kitchen: rough, curt and violent in word; nursing a howling baby amid pepper.
Croquet-ground: abruptly sugary and clinging, every remark tagged with a moral; the rough edge returns only as fear the moment the Queen appears ('A fine day, your Majesty!').

recitation_repertoire.note: Her lullaby 'Speak roughly to your little boy' (ch006-d0029, ch006-d0031) is sung text, excluded from the hit-rate denominator; it matches the kitchen-phase roughness.

backtest_markers.regex: \b(and that's (why|a fact)|don't bother|don't talk about|never could abide|that's nothing to|I make you a present)\b
^(very true|right, as usual|I quite agree|'tis so|of course it is|ah, well)\b|\b(my dear|dear old thing|tut)\b

backtest.method: marker-claim back-test: a spoken source line hits when it matches >=1 backtest_markers regex and no forbidden_words regex; verse (recited text) excluded; full definition runs/p3-dialogue-style-pb1/result.json#backtest_method
